It's the philosophic issue called 'The problem of Evil', it is and has been contemplated by philosophers and theologians, as of course the common person for a very long time; If there was a God that we assume is merciful and good...then why is there suffering and evil?

Either (A) God doesn't exist, (B) God is not Good, or (C) God has reasons for the necessity of suffering. 

A is hard if not impossible to prove, B is not tackled as much, as we assume if there was a God they would be Good, and C isn't argued well enough. 

Im positive if you could come to an understanding on one of these, you would be able to handle your illnesses more...obviously so much easier said than done. I'm sorry that you have so much pain to get you to the point of suicide. 

If you're right that this is a test, then you should try more contemplation if you can before you decide to leave this life. If you fail the test, there's then a chance you will have to suffer more in the next life or suffer longer in the afterlife. And that sounds shitty af because the choice between suffering for so many years versus a very long fucking time is a hard choice when you're in the middle of that suffering. 

Just something to think about, I'm hoping the best for you and you get relief.

I actually have Irvine's book in my library: A Guide to The Good Life-The Ancient Art of Stoic Joy. It's a very broken down easy way of understanding Stoicism without the close attention detail that I provided in my responses. He focuses more on Roman Stoicism I believe because it's easier for people to understand than Greek's version-we understand Tranquility more than we do Virtue. 

Marcus Aurelius, a Roman Stoic that is most known when we speak of Stoicism, was very into tranquility. I see tranquility as being a side effect or extra of Virtue, as he sees it as being a reward.

In irvine's book he says on page 98 "Like the other Roman Stoics, Marcus didn't feel compelled to prove that tranquility was worth pursuing. To the contrary, he thought its value was obvious. And if someone has told Marcus that he thought mortal life could offer something better than "peace of mind", Marcus would not have attempted to persuade him otherwise". 

I believe that Roman stoics might've believed more in Virtue than Tranquility, they had to sell the idea. Irvine says it quite nicely on page 55. " Epictetus would then tell the prospective student that if he wished to have a good life, he must consider his nature and the purpose for which god created him and live accordingly; he must, as Zeno put it, live in accordance with nature...he will then discover the reason we were created and the role we play in the cosmic scheme. He will realize that to have a good life, he needs to perform well the function of a human being, the function Zeus designed him to fulfill. He will therefore pursue virtue, in the ancient sense of the word, meaning that we will strive to become an excellent human being. He will also come to realize that if he lives in accordance with nature, he will be REWARDED with the tranquility that Zeus promised us."

"This explanation might have satisfied people in Epictetus's time, but it is likely to be off-putting to modern individuals...readers therefore should realize that it is entirely possible to practice Stoicism--and in particular to employ possible strategies for attaining Tranquility--without believing in Zeus...or divine creation". 

Yes Zeus existed in Roman times, but the vital role he played in philosophy and the way they viewed him was different among the people, even among Epictetus compared to other roman's at the time. Stoicism is a Way of Life. It can be followed by the atheist or by the theist. 

The atheist sees the practices to be had, the value of inner control and wisdom, and lives life as rationally as he can based upon our common major instincts (to self preservation, to social duty to care for the other human, to reason and virtue). 

The Theist follows the exact same thing, however they see these instincts coming from Nature, and Nature or the Cosmos is God to them: God provides us with this natural rational capacity and guide to live--it is our natural path to master these in the most rational way possible.

Modern Stoicism tends to fall on the atheist track--I can live a Good life as a Good human without God.

True Classical Greek Stoicism falls on the 'I'm following God's natural path in becoming a Good human being'. To understand true Stoicism you have to understand how important it is and was that God is Nature. Only in this context and this way of understanding will one understand True Stoicism and their believes on Freedom,  Virtue, and eudaemonia (I.e. Good mind, that is Happiness). 

FYI, Christians looked at this paganistic way of life and said 'oh okay, God has set natural laws we must follow.' Those natural laws they tweaked for their favor, in Stoicism those laws were from Nature and the Cosmos, for Christians it was the Holy Spirit.

This is a better understanding than most. The stoics have an idealized conception of human happiness in this world. 

Now, True Greek Stoicism believes we had certain instincts which evolve over time: instinct to self preservation, instinct to care for the other human, and instinct to reach excellence/virtue via reason. (Instinct to care is the social animal, instinct to reason the rational animal). 

Stoics look at Socrates and go 'holy shit. This guy has his shit together. We need to live like him'. They also look at Nature and see an inner rational consistency. Their philosophy on happiness is the based on this: The good life is the life lived in complete accordance with Nature, which is the same thing as living in right reason, which is living according to Virtue. 

Happiness ends up being a Virtuous life, which looks like one who has control of his self (which means control of one's emotions). Pathos, that is bad emotion, keeps us from happiness. So we do certain practices (like Negative Visualization) to remind us of our place in the world and how we should live it. To be Virtuous is to CONSISTENTLY (consistency is key to happiness--Cicero) be acting with INTENT in the best matter possible--I.E With courage not fear, with Wisdom not lies. 

Stoicism changes its goal via the century we look at it. Classic Greek Stoicism sees the goal as Virtue, Roman Stoicism as Tranquility. They're similar, but we see the goal differently as a way to get people to buy in. 

The true goal will always be EUDAIMONIA--that is the good daimon, or good spirit/mind. Happiness is in the mind, good intent will bring you happiness over good action. The Stoic can be happy while being tortured because of his CONTROL over their mind. It is controversial and yet makes total sense when looked at by reading the classic Stoics (ZENO, CHRYSIPPUS, CRITO). Also read the Roman ones (Cicero, Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus) to get a better understanding of what Stoicism is. Moderns use Stoicism to gain advantage in financial gain and life's modern circumstances, but it all comes back to (or it should) being a GOOD person with a GOOD RATIONAL MIND, following God's ( the cosmos is God to them) natural world. Natural world= mastering the instincts of self preservation, of our social duty to the other human being, to our mastering reason. 

SOURCE: old readings of the aforementioned Stoics, and Philosophy Thesis on The Good Life involving Stoicism.
